title: Keep Architecture Decisions Small Enough to Revisit
summary: Big architecture decisions are hard to undo. How to spot the one-way doors, split the rest into small records, and write down the signal that says it's time to revisit.
author: Nguyen Le Phong

faqs.q: What makes an architecture decision hard to revisit?
faqs.a: Usually its size. A single document that settles naming, boundaries, storage, ownership, rollout and migration ties many assumptions together, so changing one means reopening all of them. Splitting it into short records, one per decision that can change on its own, keeps each one easy to revisit.

faqs.q: What is a one-way door decision in software architecture?
faqs.a: The term comes from Jeff Bezos's 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders: a one-way door is consequential and irreversible or nearly so, while a two-way door can be reversed. In software, public APIs, data formats customers store and shard keys are typical one-way doors. They deserve slow review; most other decisions can move faster.

faqs.q: What should a small architecture decision record include?
faqs.a: What is decided now, what is deliberately left open, the invariant the decision protects, and the signals that should trigger a review, plus a date and an owner. When a decision is reversed, mark the old record as superseded and keep it, as Michael Nygard's ADR format suggests.

html:
Say your team is at a whiteboard that still has marks from yesterday's meeting. Someone draws three boxes, reaches for a fourth and stops. The design can clearly handle the next feature. The harder question is different: once three other teams build on what you write down today, will anyone still be able to change it?

This post is about making architecture decisions small enough to revisit: how to tell which ones are hard to undo, how to split a big decision into pieces, and what a small decision note should say so the next person knows when it's safe to change it. For the format of a decision record itself, the sibling post Architecture Decision Records for Your Future Teammates covers that. Here the focus is on size.

Most decisions are two-way doors

Jeff Bezos put the distinction neatly in his 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders. Some decisions are one-way doors: consequential and irreversible, or nearly so, and they deserve slow, careful thought. Most are two-way doors: if you got it wrong, you can walk back through. He called them Type 1 and Type 2, and warned that larger organizations tend to run the heavy Type 1 process on Type 2 decisions too. The result, in his words, is slowness, unthoughtful risk aversion and too little experimenting.

Architecture teams fall into the same trap. Martin Fowler's essay Who Needs an Architect? (IEEE Software, 2003) offers a working definition of architecture: "things that people perceive as hard to change." He then argues that one of an architect's most important jobs is to remove architecture, by finding ways to eliminate irreversibility in software designs. So the goal is to have fewer one-way decisions, and to get those few right.

Split the big decision before you write it

Some decisions get big before anyone understands them. One impressive document tries to settle naming, service boundaries, the storage model, ownership, the rollout plan and the future migration at once. It looks thorough. The catch is that it ties a dozen assumptions into one package. When one assumption changes, touching the document means reopening all the others, so nobody does.

Split it up. Each piece that can change on its own gets its own short record. Michael Nygard, who popularized architecture decision records, suggested the whole thing be one or two pages long (Documenting Architecture Decisions). Small records also make his status field work well: when a decision is reversed, you mark the old record as superseded and keep it, so the history stays readable. Superseding one small record is easy. Superseding a quarter of a giant one isn't.

A quick test when you split: for each piece, ask "if this turned out wrong in six months, what would it cost to change?" The pieces with a big answer are your one-way doors. Spend your review time there and move faster on the rest.

What a small decision says

Small doesn't mean vague. A good small decision names four things: what you're deciding now, what you're deliberately not deciding yet, the invariant it protects, and the signal that would make you look again. That last one gets skipped most often. Without it, six months later nobody knows whether the choice still fits or whether people defend it because there was once a long meeting about it.

Here's an example note. The thresholds are made up, but this is the shape:

# ADR-014: Keep tenant data behind a repository interface

Status: Accepted, 2026-10-14. Owner: platform team.

## Decision
Handlers depend on `TenantRepository`. Today it runs on PostgreSQL,
one shared schema, with `tenant_id` on every table.

## Not decided yet
Database-per-tenant, read replicas, the long-term indexing plan.

## Invariant
No query reads or writes a row without a `tenant_id` filter.

## Revisit when
- one tenant holds more than 20% of all rows, or
- a customer contract requires physical isolation, or
- the tenant list query stays above 300 ms at p95 for a week.

Notice what this does. The interface and the invariant are the load-bearing parts, written with confidence. PostgreSQL with a shared schema is today's implementation, labeled as such. The revisit list turns "we'll see" into signals someone can actually watch. A new teammate reading this knows which parts are foundations and which are scaffolding, and that's exactly what a document written in one confident voice can't tell them.

Turn one-way doors into two-way doors

Fowler's point about removing irreversibility is practical. A few habits do most of the work:

  • Put a seam in front of the expensive choice. In the example, handlers talk to an interface, so changing the storage later doesn't ripple through every use case. If you like this idea, Choose the Boundary Before You Choose the Tool goes further.
  • Decide the boundary, defer the tool. "Orders own payment status" is a boundary decision. "Use Kafka" is a tool decision that can often wait until the boundary has proven itself.
  • Roll out in a way you can roll back. A flag, a dual-write window or a shadow read keeps the old path alive while the new one earns trust.
  • Write down the exit. If a choice really is a one-way door (a public API, a data format customers store, a shard key), say so in the record and give it the slow, careful review it deserves.

Make revisiting cheap

A small decision only pays off if someone actually looks at it again. Give each record a date and an owner, link the example or incident that made it necessary, and put the revisit signals somewhere people will see them: a dashboard, an alert, a line in the quarterly planning doc. When a signal fires, open the record, write a new one if things have changed, and mark the old one superseded. That's a normal part of the work, and nobody needs to feel embarrassed about it.

The team doesn't need a perfect memory of every architecture discussion. It needs enough of a trail that the next conversation starts from the reasons, not from whatever someone remembers from the meeting.

Try this week

  • Pick your biggest current design doc. Count how many separate decisions it contains.
  • For each of them, ask what it would cost to change in six months. Mark the one-way doors.
  • Add a "Not decided yet" and a "Revisit when" section to your decision record template.
  • Choose one revisit signal and put it on a dashboard or an alert.

Small decisions don't make architecture weaker. They admit that the system will meet data, load, people and constraints nobody can see today, and they leave a handle for the next conversation. You can respect yesterday's reasoning without being stuck with yesterday's limits.
